cl_nic_vapes_harms.q: Is it safe to use a nicotine vape to quit smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_harms.short: Nobody knows for sure. In quit-smoking trials, serious health problems were about as common with nicotine vapes as with patches or gum: 7 against 6 in 100.
cl_nic_vapes_harms.but: Serious problems were few, and the trials lasted 2 years at most. That's too few and too short to show rare or later harms.
how: Health problems of any kind affected about 40 in 100 people, whether given a nicotine vape or patches or gum.
Against counselling only or no help, the evidence is weaker. Health problems of any kind: 52 in 100 with a vape against 43, which could be no real difference.
Some trials found more throat or mouth irritation, cough or dry mouth with vapes. Others found fewer breathing problems with vapes.
The trials used regulated nicotine vapes, in adults who smoked. The review says cannabis or illicit vapes may carry different harms.
cl_nic_vapes_harms.rate: Chance decided who got a vape, but serious problems were too few to rule out a small difference, and side-effect results varied between trials. The comparison with counselling or no help is weaker still.

cl_nic_pouches_stopping.q: Do nicotine pouches help people stop smoking?
cl_nic_pouches_stopping.short: Nobody knows yet. Four small trials couldn't tell whether nicotine pouches help people stop smoking or cut down. Ten more are under way.
cl_nic_pouches_stopping.but: Three of the four trials took people who weren't planning to quit, and none lasted over 8 weeks.
how: In one trial, 1 of 18 people given pouches had quit, against 0 of 9 who kept smoking.
In the same trial, 4 of 18 people given a nicotine vape had quit. Both gaps could be chance, and the trial had serious flaws.
No serious health problems were recorded in the three trials that reported them. Other side effects were mostly mild or uncommon.
One trial was paid for by a tobacco company. In it, people on pouches had lower levels of two smoke chemicals after about a week than people who kept smoking.
cl_nic_pouches_stopping.rate: Four tiny trials of 8 weeks at most, mostly in people not trying to quit, and people knew what they were given. So few people quit that any gap could be chance.

cl_nic_vapes_exposure.q: Does vaping put fewer toxic chemicals in your body than smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_exposure.short: Mostly yes. But not clearly less nicotine. In a US survey, people who only vaped had about 98% less of one cancer-linked chemical than people who only smoked.
cl_nic_vapes_exposure.but: These are chemical levels, not illness. And in surveys, people who both vaped and smoked didn't have the lower levels.
how: Short studies of people who switched to vaping found the same for most chemicals. Some were paid for by tobacco companies. The survey, paid with public money, agrees.
A UK review found nicotine wasn't clearly lower. A US expert panel judged that adults used to vaping take in about as much as from cigarettes.
People who only vaped still had more of some chemicals than people who use no tobacco or nicotine. Most had smoked for years, which may explain part of it.
cl_nic_vapes_exposure.rate: A survey at one point in time and short switching studies, some paid for by tobacco companies, all point the same way. But most people who vaped had smoked before, and these are chemical levels, not illness.

cl_nic_vapes_disease.q: Does vaping cause heart or lung disease?
cl_nic_vapes_disease.short: Nobody knows yet. A big US study found no clear rise in heart disease with vaping alone, and more lung problems that past smoking may explain.
cl_nic_vapes_disease.but: It's one study of illnesses people reported, over 4 years at most. Just 41 people who only vaped got heart disease or a stroke: too few to tell.
how: Allowing for past smoking, people who only vaped didn't clearly differ in heart disease or stroke from people who used neither. People who smoked had about 1.5 times the rate.
Lung problems like asthma or COPD: about 2.6 in 100 a year in those who had ever vaped, against 2.0 in those who hadn't. Most who vaped had smoked.
Reviews for three governments found no evidence, or too little, on heart attack, stroke, lung disease or cancer. One judged that vapes, mostly with THC, caused a lung injury outbreak.
cl_nic_vapes_disease.rate: Two analyses of one US study, based on illnesses people reported, with few heart cases among people who only vaped. Most who vaped had smoked, and nobody was followed past 4 years.

cl_nic_vapes_dependence.q: Is vaping as addictive as smoking?
cl_nic_vapes_dependence.short: Less, it seems, but still common. 77 in 100 people who only vaped daily said they felt dependent, against 94 in 100 who only smoked daily.
cl_nic_vapes_dependence.but: Nearly all who vaped had smoked before. And this US survey is from 2013 to 2014, before disposables and newer liquids were common.
how: In the same survey, fewer who only vaped had strong cravings: 73 against 87 in 100.
Other surveys agreed. In England, about half of 16- to 19-year-olds who vaped said they felt at least a little dependent, against 83 in 100 who smoked.
One web survey asked what people used. Bigger, more advanced vapes and liquids with more nicotine went with higher dependence scores.
Expert reviews in the US and Australia judged that vaping can lead to dependence. The US panel judged, less firmly, that the risk is lower than with smoking.
cl_nic_vapes_dependence.rate: One-time surveys of what people said, with no follow-up. Nearly all who vaped had smoked before, past smoking wasn't allowed for, and the surveys came before newer vapes like disposables were common.

cl_nic_vapes_nearby.short: Nobody knows yet. No study we read checked their health. Vaping does add nicotine and tiny particles to the air, but less than cigarette smoke.
cl_nic_vapes_nearby.but: The studies were small and lasted minutes to hours. Nobody followed people nearby for weeks or years.
how: A US expert panel describes studies in test rooms and homes. The more people vaped, the more nicotine and tiny particles were in the air.
After short spells near vaping, tests found no change in the body. Long, heavy vaping nearby, or living with someone who vaped, went with more nicotine or other chemicals.
Some may be at special risk, the panel adds. It names children, pregnant women, older people and people with heart or lung disease.
A Dutch computer model of worst cases found small safety margins for some chemicals, like nicotine in a car. Its authors called the effects fairly mild.
cl_nic_vapes_nearby.rate: Small, short studies of the air and of a few people's body levels, mostly from 2014 to 2017, plus computer models. None of the studies we read measured the health of people nearby.
